Each \(T\)-tetromino covers \(4\) squares.

### 1. Upper bound

Since the grid has \(36\) squares, the area bound gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{36}{4}\right\rfloor=9.
\]

However, \(9\) tetrominoes would have to cover the entire grid. Color the grid like a checkerboard, with \(18\) black and \(18\) white squares.

Every \(T\)-tetromino covers three squares of one color and one square of the other. If \(k\) of nine pieces cover three black squares, then the total number of covered black squares would be
\[
3k+(9-k)=9+2k,
\]
which is odd. It therefore cannot equal the \(18\) black squares of the board. Thus nine pieces are impossible, so at most eight can be placed.

### 2. Construction with eight pieces

The following arrangement works; equal letters form one \(T\)-tetromino, and dots are unused squares:

\[
\begin{array}{cccccc}
A&A&A&B&E&\cdot\\
D&A&B&B&E&E\\
D&D&C&B&E&F\\
D&C&C&C&F&F\\
G&G&G&\cdot&H&F\\
\cdot&G&\cdot&H&H&H
\end{array}
\]

Each of \(A,B,\ldots,H\) forms a rotated \(T\)-tetromino, so eight nonoverlapping pieces can indeed be placed.
